svg.text: MPx Boil-Loop · Ergonomics on an Indian kitchen counter (preliminary)
Side elevation, 1:10 scale feel. Counter and cabinet heights from Indian kitchen practice; body dimensions should be checked against Chakrabarti (1997) percentiles before freezing.
A · Side elevation: counter, wall cabinet, user
Indian guidance puts the counter-to-cabinet gap at ≥ 600 mm. At 420 mm tall the unit leaves
~180 mm, enough to lift the filter (~110 mm) and the tank straight up.
Indian platforms run 810–915 mm, most often ~860 mm. Display and keys then sit ~1.28 m above
the floor, below eye level for most adults, so the cap chamfer faces up at 30°.
160 mm clear above the grate fits steel tumblers and 500 mL bottles; lifting out the grate
gives ~175 mm. 1 L bottles need a jug or a tilt.
1.5 L water + ~0.45 kg glass ≈ 2 kg, single-hand lift from the side, well under the 50 N
ceiling in req 3.1/8.2. Handle opening ≥ 90 × 35 mm; verify against hand-breadth data.
Shell ~28 °C at 25 °C room (sim S6), under the 48 °C limit for metal held > 1 min (IEC
62368-1 / ISO 13732-1). Core is 100 °C but insulated and interlocked.
Top hatch stays locked while the calm zone is above 50 °C; filter lifted by an insulated
Fill tank → press Start → take cup when the ring turns blue. Meets req 8.3 (≤ 3 steps). First
water ~17 min after a cold start.
Two capacitive keys ≥ 15 mm, 20 mm apart, plus app. Simple vs detailed display mode (req
Peristaltic pump is quiet; the simmer is the loudest part. Measure against ≤ 60 dB(A) at 1 m
~5.3 kg dry: a countertop appliance, not portable. Two finger recesses under the base for
Sources: housing.com (cabinet gap ≥ 600 mm); houseyog.com (platform 810–915 mm); UL tech brief on IEC 62368-1
touch limits; Chakrabarti D. (1997) Indian Anthropometric Dimensions, NID.
